report:
**Conclusion: The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is not supported by the current scientific consensus.**

The waxes commonly used on apples — carnauba wax, shellac, and beeswax — all carry FDA "Generally Recognized As Safe" (GRAS) status. These waxes are biologically inert, meaning the human digestive system cannot break them down, and they pass through without harm. The prevailing scientific consensus is that carnauba wax does not cause cancer ([Advance Study](https://advancestudy.org/does-carnauba-wax-cause-cancer/); [Biology Insights](https://biologyinsights.com/is-carnauba-wax-safe-to-eat-and-is-it-good-for-you/)).

The Harvard/Dana-Farber Cancer FactFinder — a tool developed by experts at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Dana-Farber Cancer Center — directly addresses this claim. It concludes: "Coatings on fruits and vegetables are not dangerous under FDA and EPA guidelines, but rinsing off or peeling produce helps to remove the wax" ([Cancer FactFinder](https://cancerfactfinder.org/diet-nutrition/wax-on-fruits-and-vegetables/)).

**However, there are legitimate secondary concerns worth noting:**

- **Pesticide trapping:** Wax coatings can trap pesticide residues on the apple surface. Some pesticides have been linked to cancer risk, though washing or peeling mitigates this ([Non-Toxic Dad](https://nontoxicdad.com/solutions/why-you-need-to-wash-the-wax-off-your-apples/)).
- **Morpholine:** Some wax formulations use morpholine as a solvent. When combined with nitrite, it can form nitrosomorpholine, a genotoxic carcinogen in rodents. The EU has banned morpholine in wax coatings, though the FDA permits it at low levels considered safe ([Food Policy for Canada](https://foodpolicyforcanada.info.yorku.ca/solutions-intro-additives/)).

**Bottom line:** The wax itself does not cause cancer. To address residual concerns, wash apples thoroughly with water (or a baking soda solution) or peel them before eating.
